The more bits, the more memory the processor can address, and also the more data it can process at a time.

In short, it is the size of the number the cpu can process. 64 bits can hold a ton more info than 32 bits. The biggest benefit of this for most people is that it allows you to use more memory (from a 4gb cap to an exabyte cap). It also has significant benefits in terms of data processing applications (encryption, encoding, etc.). The 64-bit wiki page does a better job of explaining tbh

32-bit and 64-bit refers to the length of memory (i.e. RAM) addresses. A 32-bit address can have 2^32 = 4GB unique values, which is why 32-bit processors can only support up to 4GB of memory. This is obviously a severe restriction, given that a lot of computers nowadays have at least 8GB of memory. So they made 64-bit processors, which can theoretically support up to 16ExaByte (i.e. roughly 16,000,000,000 TB) of memory. Since we are nowhere near having that much RAM yet, we don't need to have anything more than 64-bit processors.

I should also mention that chipmakers had to redesign a great deal of things about processors to make 64-bit addresses work. In particular, the 64-bit architecture involve more expensive parts (64-bit registers, larger CPU caches, etc. if you know what I'm talking about), so that's why we don't have 128-bit processors. Why don't we just make 33(or any number between 32 and 64)-bit processors to cut costs? My understanding is that having 64-bit addresses allows two 32-bit values to fit inside a single 64-bit values. If you used a, say, 33-bit address, one bit would be wasted by programs that still use 32-bit values. That wastage is kinda significant at the CPU level. But I may be wrong; if so someone please correct me.

I've posted this a couple of times here... but a lot of the 'dives' you see are legit.

In short, you can't trip a player in a soccer. You can't step on their feet or anything... that is a legit foul.

So when that happens, players will often drop to the ground to get the ref to call the foul. Otherwise they run the risk of the ref assuming the player doesn't want the foul called. This is called, "Playing the advantage".

So the player is more then often fouled, just not bad enough to actually be tripped... but he trips and falls anyway because that's how you tell the ref you want the foul called. The ref doesn't always agree though and sometimes a player goes down to the ground easy, and gets no call.
